newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan aims to be regional money centre.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan aims to be regional money centre.

text.p: Taiwan is grooming itself as a top Asia-Pacific capital market and has the industrial and financial muscle to succeed despite political isolation imposed by rival China, Finance Minister Paul Chiu said on Tuesday.
Chiu, in an interview with Reuters Financial Television, said Taiwan had advantages of economic scale and depth that rival money centres Singapore and Hong Kong could not match.
But he acknowledged that China's sometimes dramatic efforts to contain what it regards as a renegade province posed obstacles to Taiwan's efforts to cultivate regional financial markets.
Chiu, who holds a doctorate in monetary economics from Ohio State University, said his goals as finance minister were to streamline the tax system and regionalise the money market.

"By the year 2000 all of our cross-border capital movement controls will be removed," Chiu said in fluent English. "By the year 2000 I think we should be able to compete effectively with the Hong Kong and Singapore markets."
Chiu added that the liberalisation of cross-border capital movements did not apply to communist China, Taiwan's arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949.
Whether Taipei's restrictions on Taiwan-China capital flows will end by 2000 would depend very much on progress towards reunification, a process that ground to a halt in mid-1995.

Noting that the central bank and other agencies had acted aggressively to defend Taiwan's currency and financial stability during a military crisis with China that peaked in March, Chiu said Taipei would do so again if necessary.
"I think we would still do these kinds of things if a similar kind of military exercise conducted by mainland China happened once again," he said.
Chiu, who became finance minister in June, was central bank vice governor in March and helped direct its US$10 billion defence that held the Taiwan dollar at T$27.5 to the U.S. unit.

Chiu said Taiwan's capital market was buoyed by a high savings rate, a healthy ratio between money supply and economic growth and a powerful manufacturing and export economy -- particularly in high-technology products and electronics.

"These strong manufacturing sectors create demand for funds as well as a supply of funds. That is our strength," he said. "We will continue these strengths to develop Taiwan into an asset management centre."
Singapore had advantages due to its offshore banking units and Hong Kong with its intimate links to China's huge economy, but neither compared with Taiwan's economic size and diversity.

The Asian Development Bank and other international agencies already are tapping Taiwan's huge money market, and reforms are being pursued to end rules that keep brokerages from managing funds, which will enlarge Taiwan's capital pool, he said.

Chiu said a "two-into-one" income tax reform to end double taxation was unlikely to face parliamentary opposition and could take effect in January 1998 in a cabinet-wide bid to jumpstart a slowing economy by improving Taiwan's investment climate.
The drive to become an Asia-Pacific money centre is part of an ambitious plan to build Taiwan into a base for transnational firms' regional operations centres.

An easing of tensions with China would improve Taiwan's prospects for financing projects across the Asia-Pacific region -- including on the Chinese mainland -- but better economic ties with China were not essential to the capital market scheme.
"We cannot really rely on relations with mainland China as a prerequisite for development of the Taiwan regional operations centre," he said.
